paragraphs.text: The example’s outbox table has event_id as its primary key, a required order_id reference and required payload. Scheduling and ownership add five columns:

The candidate query locks the row it selects; the update gives that claim a deadline and a generation. The returned token is provisional until the worker receives a successful commit reply. If that reply is missing, this protocol abandons the claim: discard its token and never use it to call the receiver, renew the lease or record completion. Dispose of the broken connection and finish its cleanup. Resume polling through the normal claim query, accepting a claim only when its commit succeeds. If the uncertain claim did commit, its lease keeps the event unavailable until expiry; this deliberately trades some recovery time for a simpler ownership contract.

A matching token in a later lookup cannot recover that ownership. A can receive token 1 before commit, then disconnect and have its update rolled back. B can then commit a claim with token 1. Locking the row now reveals B’s current lease, even though its number matches A’s discarded token. The increment orders committed claims of this event; it does not identify every attempted claim.

If a job needs more time, renew only a claim whose commit was acknowledged, while its token still matches and its lease is unexpired. Wait for the renewal’s successful commit reply before continuing. If renewal changes no row or its outcome becomes uncertain, abandon the claim and stop starting work under it. This does not recall a network request already sent.
The worker calls the receiver after its claim’s commit was acknowledged. On a confirmed receiver success, it records completion with the event ID and that claim’s token:

A returned row and successful commit reply confirm completion. No row means the claim expired, was replaced or was already completed. Do not turn it into an unconditional update. The token prevents an old worker from marking a later worker’s claim complete. If completion’s reply is missing, retire the claim as well: do no further work under it. A committed completion removes the event from polling; otherwise lease expiry allows another claim to recover it.

The native experiment held an uncommitted claim while another worker polled: the second skipped the locked row. After the claim committed, its active lease excluded the event. The test then explicitly moved the deadline into the past to model expiry. B obtained token 2; A’s completion with token 1 changed zero rows, while B’s completion changed one. It also reproduced A’s rolled-back token 1 matching B’s committed token 1. The worker discarded A’s uncertain claim in that history and in a second history where A’s commit succeeded but its reply was withheld; neither authorised a receiver call, renewal or completion. Normal polling recovered the unfinished event.

Retry temporary failures with bounded backoff and jitter, carrying the same event and effect identities. Set available_at for a later attempt and release the lease only under an acknowledged claim whose token still matches and whose lease is unexpired. Abandon the claim if this update’s outcome becomes uncertain. Retain the attempt count and useful error information. Stop retrying a permanently invalid payload as though elapsed time will repair it.

paragraphs.text: The example’s outbox table has event_id as its primary key, a required order_id reference and required payload. Scheduling and ownership add five columns:

The candidate query locks the row it selects; the update gives that claim a deadline and a generation. The returned token is provisional until the worker receives a successful commit reply. If that reply is missing, this protocol abandons the claim: discard its token and never use it to call the receiver, renew the lease or record completion. Dispose of the broken connection and finish its cleanup. Resume polling through the normal claim query, accepting a claim only when its commit succeeds. If the uncertain claim did commit, its lease keeps the event unavailable until expiry; this deliberately trades some recovery time for a simpler ownership contract.

A matching token in a later lookup cannot recover that ownership. A can receive token 1 before commit, then disconnect and have its update rolled back. B can then commit a claim with token 1. Locking the row now reveals B’s current lease, even though its number matches A’s discarded token. The increment orders committed claims of this event; it does not identify every attempted claim.

If a job needs more time, renew only a claim whose commit was acknowledged, while its token still matches and its lease is unexpired. Wait for the renewal’s successful commit reply before continuing. If renewal changes no row or its outcome becomes uncertain, abandon the claim and stop starting work under it. This does not recall a network request already sent.
The worker calls the receiver after its claim’s commit was acknowledged. On a confirmed receiver success, it records completion with the event ID and that claim’s token:

A returned row and successful commit reply confirm completion. No row means the claim expired, was replaced or was already completed. Do not turn it into an unconditional update. The token prevents an old worker from marking a later worker’s claim complete. If completion’s reply is missing, retire the claim as well: do no further work under it. A committed completion removes the event from polling; otherwise lease expiry allows another claim to recover it.

The native experiment held an uncommitted claim while another worker polled: the second skipped the locked row. After the claim committed, its active lease excluded the event. The test then explicitly moved the deadline into the past to model expiry. B obtained token 2; A’s completion with token 1 changed zero rows, while B’s completion changed one. It also reproduced A’s rolled-back token 1 matching B’s committed token 1. The worker discarded A’s uncertain claim in that history and in a second history where A’s commit succeeded but its reply was withheld; neither authorised a receiver call, renewal or completion. Normal polling recovered the unfinished event.

Retry temporary failures with bounded backoff and jitter, carrying the same event and effect identities. Set available_at for a later attempt and release the lease only under an acknowledged claim whose token still matches and whose lease is unexpired. Abandon the claim if this update’s outcome becomes uncertain. Retain the attempt count and useful error information. Stop retrying a permanently invalid payload as though elapsed time will repair it.

The recorded PostgreSQL 18.6 run checks the separate-write gap, combined commit and rollback, locked-row skipping, active leases, abandoned uncertain claims, injected expiry, newer claims, stale completion, duplicate effects, receiver fencing and atomic consumer receipts. It terminates an owned client before commit and withholds selected successful replies from a simulated worker. These are controlled fault injections, alongside modelled worker pauses and omitted follow-up writes. They do not measure a network failure, lease duration, production throughput, broker delivery or a provider’s service contract.
